To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

co-emitted cues are integrated as early as 170 ms and this integration depends on the attentional load of the observer, as the neural sources of this early integration differ as a function of attentional load.

(i) co-emitted social visual cues are combined in the brain at the same timing, regardless of the task relevance of the cues, (ii) the relative contribution of different neural sources to this integration is modulated by the attended feature.
co-emitted cues are integrated even if they are not task relevant, and that the relative contribution of different neural sources of integration depends on the attended feature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early integration of social cues in a multimodal context, with the aim of understanding the neural mechanisms underlying the combination of social signals.
the early integration of multiple social signals.
the neural bases of early combination of co-emitted visual social signals and the role of attention in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the integration of social cues is a general process that is modulated by the attended feature.
the neural sources involved in the integration of social cues depend on the task relevance of the attended feature.

the early integration of social cues, which occurs at the level of the superior temporal sulcus, is not affected by selective attention, and that the relative contribution of the different sources involved in this integration is modulated by the task relevance of the attended cue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selective attention modulates the neural sources of integration of co-emitted signals, even when they do not need to be combined to perform the task at hand.

selective attention effects on the early integration of social cues are not due to a top-down modulation of sensory processing, but are rather related to a change in the neural sources that are involved in social integration processes.

selective attention modulates the integration of social cues by changing the relative contribution of neural sources, which is in line with the view that social cues are integrated in a flexible and adaptive way to optimize social interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selective attention to a specific social cue impacts on the integration of co-emitted cues, as the integration process is modulated by the attended cue.
social signals are integrated in a flexible way, depending on the attended social cue.
the integration of social cues is not an all-or-none phenomenon, but it is highly dependent on the observer's attention.
